Lessons.Title: Related Events
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Define independent and dependent events correctly by whether knowing one changes the probability of the other, and test independence from joint probability.
Two events A and B are independent exactly when P(A∩B)=P(A)×P(B). If P(B)>0, this is equivalent to P(A|B)=P(A): knowing B occurred does not change A's probability.

Dependence means the conditional probability differs from the unconditional probability: P(A|B)≠P(A) when P(B)>0. Disjoint events with positive probabilities are not independent, because P(A∩B)=0 while P(A)×P(B)>0.

Original student task: Use a two-stage card model and explain why replacement changes independence; teacher scores experimental plan. Teacher rubric (0–4): explicit event/model definitions, appropriate denominators, correct calculations, and justified claims including sampling limits. Experiments and written discussion require human scoring.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 8 Lesson 7, CC BY 4.0. Original Edulytiks examples; no copied licensed artwork or restricted assessment responses.

KeyConcepts.Title: Independence
KeyConcepts.Rule: For P(B)>0, independence is equivalent to P(A|B)=P(A).
KeyConcepts.Example: Two independent fair coin tosses: P(first head | second head)=1/2=P(first head).

KeyConcepts.Title: Dependence
KeyConcepts.Definition: Conditioning on B changes A probability
KeyConcepts.Rule: For P(B)>0, dependence occurs when P(A|B)≠P(A).
KeyConcepts.Example: With two red and one blue card drawn without replacement, P(red second | red first)=1/2, versus unconditional P(red second)=2/3.

KeyConcepts.Title: Disjoint versus independent
KeyConcepts.Definition: Positive-probability disjoint events cannot be independent
KeyConcepts.Example: Fair die rolls 1 vs 2 on same roll

WorkedExamples.Title: Related Events: model 1
WorkedExamples.Question: Fair coin twice; A=first head, B=second head. Independent?
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify probabilities lie within [0,1] and condition event probability is positive when applicable.

WorkedExamples.Title: Related Events: model 2
WorkedExamples.Question: Draw two cards without replacement from deck with 2 red, 1 blue. Is red first independent of red second?
Steps: By symmetry, P(second red)=2/3 before learning the first draw.
After the first draw is red, one red and one blue card remain; thus P(second red | first red)=1/2.
The positive conditioned probability 1/2 is unequal to unconditional 2/3, so the events are dependent.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify probabilities lie within [0,1] and condition event probability is positive when applicable.

WorkedExamples.Title: Related Events: model 3
WorkedExamples.Question: Two disjoint events each probability 1/4. Can they be independent?
Steps: Intersection=0
Product P(A)P(B)=1/16>0
Independence equality fails
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify probabilities lie within [0,1] and condition event probability is positive when applicable.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Defining independence as one event affecting another
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use P(A∩B)=P(A)×P(B), or P(A|B)=P(A) for P(B)>0; changing the probability under a condition means dependence.

SummaryPoints: Define independent and dependent events correctly by whether knowing one changes the probability of the other, and test independence from joint probability.
For P(B)>0, independence means P(A|B)=P(A), equivalently P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). Disjoint positive-probability events are dependent.

Lessons.Title: Conditional Probability
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Compute conditional probability with restricted sample space and derive multiplication formula for joint events.
When the conditioning event B has positive probability, P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B). Only outcomes in B remain in the conditioned sample space; the numerator counts those also in A.
The multiplication formula P(A∩B)=P(A|B)P(B) applies whenever P(B)>0 and does not assume independence. If P(B)=0, the elementary conditional quotient P(A|B) is undefined; do not divide by zero.

Original student task: Students redraw a restricted sample space and derive the multiplication identity from count ratios; teacher reviews proof. Teacher rubric (0–4): explicit event/model definitions, appropriate denominators, correct calculations, and justified claims including sampling limits. Experiments and written discussion require human scoring.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 8 Lesson 8, CC BY 4.0. Original Edulytiks examples; no copied licensed artwork or restricted assessment responses.

KeyConcepts.Title: Conditional formula
KeyConcepts.Definition: For P(B)>0, the probability of A given B is the proportion of outcomes in B that also belong to A.
KeyConcepts.Example: If P(A∩B)=0.2 and P(B)=0.4, then P(A|B)=0.5.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiplication rule
KeyConcepts.Definition: The joint event probability equals the conditional probability of A given B multiplied by the probability of B.
KeyConcepts.Rule: P(A∩B)=P(A|B)×P(B) when P(B)>0; no independence assumption is needed.
KeyConcepts.Example: If P(A|B)=0.3 and P(B)=0.5, the joint probability is 0.15.

KeyConcepts.Title: Zero-probability condition
KeyConcepts.Definition: Elementary conditional ratio not defined when P(B)=0
KeyConcepts.Example: For P(B)=0, the elementary ratio P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/0 is undefined; this does not mean its value is 0.

WorkedExamples.Title: Conditional Probability: model 1
WorkedExamples.Question: P(A∩B)=0.2 and P(B)=0.4. Find P(A|B).
Steps: The condition is event B, whose probability is P(B)=0.4>0.
The conditional probability is 0.5.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify probabilities lie within [0,1] and condition event probability is positive when applicable.

WorkedExamples.Title: Conditional Probability: model 2
WorkedExamples.Question: P(B)=0.5 and P(A|B)=0.3. Find joint probability.
Steps: Use the general multiplication rule P(A∩B)=P(A|B)×P(B).
Substitute P(A|B)=0.3 and P(B)=0.5.
Multiply 0.3×0.5=0.15 to obtain the joint probability.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify probabilities lie within [0,1] and condition event probability is positive when applicable.

WorkedExamples.Title: Conditional Probability: model 3
WorkedExamples.Question: A fair die result is even given that result exceeds 3. Find P(even|>3).
Steps: Given that the die result is greater than 3, the equally likely outcomes are {4,5,6}.
Of these, {4,6} are even, so exactly two of three conditioned outcomes meet the event.
Therefore P(even | result>3)=2/3.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify probabilities lie within [0,1] and condition event probability is positive when applicable.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Dividing by P(A) when given B
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Conditional denominator must match after bar
CommonMistakes.Correction: In P(A|B), divide the joint probability P(A∩B) by P(B); P(B|A) has the different denominator P(A).
Check P(B)>0 before computing P(A|B); when P(B)=0 the elementary conditional probability is undefined.

SummaryPoints: Compute conditional probability with restricted sample space and derive multiplication formula for joint events.
For P(B)>0, P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) and P(A∩B)=P(A|B)×P(B); neither equation requires independence.
Source-specific probability models and experimental interpretations require teacher review.

Lessons.Title: Using Tables for Conditional Probability
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Compute row-conditional and column-conditional probabilities from a frequency table and distinguish them from marginals.
Given event A in a two-way table, P(B|A)=count(A∩B)/count(A) when count(A)>0; the denominator is the A row total. The marginal P(B)=count(B)/N uses the grand total instead.
Given B, the reversed conditional P(A|B)=count(A∩B)/count(B) when count(B)>0. To check independence in the empirical table distribution, compare P(B|A) with P(B), or test P(A∩B)=P(A)×P(B).

Original student task: Use an original school-club hypothetical contingency table, justify population and limitations; teacher scores model. Teacher rubric (0–4): explicit event/model definitions, appropriate denominators, correct calculations, and justified claims including sampling limits. Experiments and written discussion require human scoring.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 8 Lesson 9, CC BY 4.0. Original Edulytiks examples; no copied licensed artwork or restricted assessment responses.

KeyConcepts.Title: Conditional row
KeyConcepts.Definition: Given A, denominator is total count of row A
KeyConcepts.Example: For [[12,8],[18,12]], the A row has 20 observations, so P(B|A)=12/20=0.6.

KeyConcepts.Title: Conditional column
KeyConcepts.Definition: Given B, denominator is total count column B
KeyConcepts.Example: The B column has 30 observations, so P(A|B)=12/30=0.4.

KeyConcepts.Title: Independence table test
KeyConcepts.Definition: If P(A)>0, compare P(B|A) with the marginal P(B), or compare joint P(A∩B) against P(A)×P(B).
KeyConcepts.Rule: P(B|A)=P(B) for P(A)>0 if and only if A and B are independent.
KeyConcepts.Example: The table gives P(B|A)=12/20=0.6 and P(B)=30/50=0.6, so A and B are independent in its empirical distribution.

WorkedExamples.Title: Using Tables for Conditional Probability: model 1
WorkedExamples.Question: Table A/B counts [[12,8],[18,12]]: compute P(B|A).
Steps: Condition on A: its row contains count(A)=12+8=20 observations.
The count in both A and B is count(A∩B)=12.
Therefore P(B|A)=12/20=0.6.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify probabilities lie within [0,1] and condition event probability is positive when applicable.

WorkedExamples.Title: Using Tables for Conditional Probability: model 2
WorkedExamples.Question: Same table: compute P(A|B).
Steps: Condition on B: its column contains count(B)=12+18=30 observations.
The intersection A∩B still contains 12 observations.
Therefore P(A|B)=12/30=0.4.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify probabilities lie within [0,1] and condition event probability is positive when applicable.

WorkedExamples.Title: Using Tables for Conditional Probability: model 3
WorkedExamples.Question: Are A and B independent in this table?
Steps: There are N=50 observations, so P(A)=20/50=0.4.
Since P(A)×P(B)=0.4×0.6=0.24=P(A∩B), events are independent in the table's empirical distribution.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes, for the empirical distribution represented.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify probabilities lie within [0,1] and condition event probability is positive when applicable.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using grand total for every conditional denominator
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A given condition restricts sample space
P(A|B) conditions on B (column count); P(B|A) conditions on A (row count). Their denominators and values can differ.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Read the event after the vertical bar as the condition: P(A|B)=12/30=0.4, but P(B|A)=12/20=0.6 in this table.

SummaryPoints: Compute row-conditional and column-conditional probabilities from a frequency table and distinguish them from marginals.
For this table P(B|A)=12/20=0.6, P(A|B)=12/30=0.4, and joint P(A∩B)=12/50=0.24; do not interchange denominators.
Source-specific probability models and experimental interpretations require teacher review.

Lessons.Title: Using Probability to Determine Whether Events Are Independent
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Test independence from observed proportions, conditional probabilities and uncertainty from finite samples.
In an exact probability model, A and B are independent if and only if P(A∩B)=P(A)×P(B). Check joint, marginal and conditional probabilities with their named events and valid denominators.
For P(B)>0, the equivalent criterion is P(A|B)=P(A). Empirical frequencies from a finite classroom sample are estimates and cannot by themselves prove population-level independence or dependence.

Original student task: Design a hypothetical data collection with two binary variables and discuss sampling uncertainty; teacher reviews critique. Teacher rubric (0–4): explicit event/model definitions, appropriate denominators, correct calculations, and justified claims including sampling limits. Experiments and written discussion require human scoring.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 8 Lesson 10, CC BY 4.0. Original Edulytiks examples; no copied licensed artwork or restricted assessment responses.

KeyConcepts.Title: Joint-product criterion
KeyConcepts.Definition: For events A,B, independence iff P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B)
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use exact model probabilities where available

KeyConcepts.Title: Conditional criterion
KeyConcepts.Definition: If P(B)>0, the events are independent precisely when learning that B occurred leaves A's probability unchanged.
KeyConcepts.Rule: P(A|B)=P(A) if and only if A and B are independent, provided P(B)>0.
KeyConcepts.Example: If P(A)=0.4 and P(A|B)=0.3, with P(B)>0, the events are dependent.

KeyConcepts.Title: Sampling uncertainty
KeyConcepts.Definition: Empirical counts estimate underlying probability, not prove population independence

WorkedExamples.Title: Using Probability to Determine Whether Events Are Independent: model 1
WorkedExamples.Question: Model P(A)=0.4,P(B)=0.5,joint=0.2. Independent?
Steps: Compute product 0.4·0.5=0.2
Compare with given joint 0.2
Equality holds
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes, in the stated probability model.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify probabilities lie within [0,1] and condition event probability is positive when applicable.

WorkedExamples.Title: Using Probability to Determine Whether Events Are Independent: model 2
WorkedExamples.Question: Model P(A)=0.4,P(A|B)=0.3 with P(B)>0. Independent?
Steps: With P(B)>0, independence would require P(A|B)=P(A).
The given P(A|B)=0.3 differs from P(A)=0.4.
Therefore the events are dependent in this probability model.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify probabilities lie within [0,1] and condition event probability is positive when applicable.

WorkedExamples.Title: Using Probability to Determine Whether Events Are Independent: model 3
WorkedExamples.Question: A 20-trial classroom frequency table suggests rates 0.5 and 0.55. Does it prove population independence?
Steps: Frequencies are sample estimates
Sample fluctuation can create small differences
Without inferential assumptions cannot prove underlying relationship
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify probabilities lie within [0,1] and condition event probability is positive when applicable.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating small relative frequency differences as conclusive population dependence
CommonMistakes.Correction: Separate empirical evidence from formal model equality

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming independence whenever events can occur together
CommonMistakes.Correction: Events can overlap and still be dependent; use P(A∩B)=P(A)×P(B), or the proper conditional equality with a positive conditioning probability.

SummaryPoints: Test independence from observed proportions, conditional probabilities and uncertainty from finite samples.
In an exact probability model, independence means P(A∩B)=P(A)×P(B), or P(A|B)=P(A) when P(B)>0.
Source-specific probability models and experimental interpretations require teacher review.

Lessons.Title: Probabilities in Games
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: optional source practice collecting and interpreting classroom game trials to estimate conditional probabilities and determine independence, while distinguishing data estimates from an exact chance model.
A symmetric payout game is fair in expectation when mean net gain equals zero Weight all outcomes by their probabilities

Source-specific experiment: in a three-card bag with two red cards and one blue card, compare probabilities of red on a second draw with and without replacement. Without replacement the second-draw probability depends on the first draw; with replacement the conditional red probability remains 2/3 on each draw. Specify recorded counts and use the table's actual conditioning denominators.

Without replacement, a first red draw leaves one red and one blue card, changing the next red probability to 1/2. With replacement, the second draw retains probability 2/3 even after observing a first red; exact model independence differs from fluctuating classroom frequencies.

Original student task: Students design a noncommercial, classroom probability board game with mathematical payoffs and critique whether repeated rounds are independent. Teacher scores rules, modelling and evidence. Teacher rubric (0–4): explicit event/model definitions, appropriate denominators, correct calculations, and justified claims including sampling limits. Experiments and written discussion require human scoring.
Source: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 8 Lesson 11, CC BY 4.0. Original Edulytiks examples; no copied licensed artwork or restricted assessment responses.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fairness
KeyConcepts.Definition: A symmetric payout game is fair in expectation when mean net gain equals zero
KeyConcepts.Rule: Weight all outcomes by their probabilities
KeyConcepts.Example: Win $2 with probability 1/3 and lose $1 with probability 2/3 gives EV=0

KeyConcepts.Title: Game independence
KeyConcepts.Definition: Separate rounds require a mechanism that does not alter later probabilities
KeyConcepts.Rule: Replacing cards may help ensure repeated-round independence

KeyConcepts.Title: Expected value
KeyConcepts.Rule: Positive expected net gain favors player long term under model

WorkedExamples.Title: Probabilities in Games: model 1
WorkedExamples.Question: Game wins $2 with probability 1/3, loses $1 otherwise. Is expected net gain fair?
Steps: Expected gain (1/3)·2=2/3
Expected loss (2/3)·(−1)=−2/3
Adding the two weighted outcomes gives expected net gain 2/3−2/3=0.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify probabilities lie within [0,1] and condition event probability is positive when applicable.

WorkedExamples.Title: Probabilities in Games: conditional draw model
WorkedExamples.Question: A bag contains two red cards and one blue. Draw without replacement. Find P(second red | first red).
WorkedExamples.Method: Condition on the first observed result and count remaining equally likely cards.
Steps: After first red, two cards remain: one red and one blue.
The conditioned sample has two equally likely cards.
Only one is red, so probability of red on second draw given first red is 1/2.
WorkedExamples.Check: Unconditional P(second red)=2/3 by symmetry, so this demonstrates dependence.

WorkedExamples.Title: Probabilities in Games: replacement changes independence
WorkedExamples.Question: A bag contains two red cards and one blue. After each draw, replace the selected card. Find P(second red | first red), and explain dependence.
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute the conditional sample space after replacement.
Steps: After the first red card is returned, all three cards remain: two red and one blue.
Given the first result, the next draw still gives red with probability 2/3.
P(second red | first red)=2/3 equals unconditional P(second red)=2/3, so the draws are independent under this with-replacement model.
WorkedExamples.Answer: P(second red | first red)=2/3; successive draws are independent with replacement.
WorkedExamples.Check: Contrast with without-replacement conditional probability 1/2 after a first red.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling a game fair because win and lose names each appear once

CommonMistakes.Correction: Use exact model EV and report empirical frequencies separately

SummaryPoints: Classroom game data provide empirical estimates of conditional probabilities and evidence about independence; do not treat a small experimental sample as mathematical proof of the population model.
Weight all outcomes by their probabilities
Source-specific probability models and experimental interpretations require teacher review.
